strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation: Compelling argument that object-level scene graphs are too coarse; part-level relations address genuine limitations in existing representations
Clear and expressive PAG representation: Two-level hierarchy with object and part nodes is intuitive; DAG structure naturally enforces physical realizability and assembly ordering
Substantial dataset contribution: PARSE-10K fills a real gap with 10,000 scenes, part-level segmentation, and contact graphs across 132 object categories and 17 room types
Practical and well-designed solver: Coarse-to-fine constraint satisfaction approach is sensible; clear algorithmic description with effective examples showing progressive refinement
Strong experimental results: 97.4% accuracy on visual relation MCQ (vs. 86.2% for best baseline), 86.2% on part-level contact; user study shows 47.5% preference for PAG-conditioned generation
Quality presentation: Well-organized paper with informative figures effectively illustrating PAG structure and solver mechanics
Comprehensive comparison of datasets: Table 1 clearly demonstrates PARSE-10K's unique advantages over existing resources in terms of part annotations and contact structures
weaknesses: Critically underspecified PAG construction: Real-image layout prior extraction is mentioned but barely explained; process for converting images to PAGs is essentially a black box; percentage requiring manual construction and annotation cost are vague

Limited algorithmic novelty: Solver uses standard constraint satisfaction techniques (coarse-to-fine refinement, iterative constraint accumulation); physics simulation is off-the-shelf; novelty is primarily in representation design and dataset rather than methods

Incomplete experimental evaluation: VLM comparisons are against general-purpose models rather than specialized spatial reasoning baselines; only one baseline (InstructScene) for scene generation; no ablations isolating contribution of part-level annotations

Contact model limitations not quantified: Directional-face model acknowledged to deviate on oblique contacts but no failure rate analysis provided; no alternative contact representations evaluated; impacts realism for certain object types unexplored
Missing ablation studies: No ablations on DAG structure, edge type importance, hierarchical organization, or solver stage contributions; sensitivity to constraint ordering not analyzed

Insufficient dataset analysis: Limited breakdown of diversity (17 room types mentioned but not listed); no analysis of relation type distribution; potential biases from real-image sources not discussed

Reproducibility gaps: Algorithm details sparse (constraint formulations, numerical tolerances, convergence criteria); hyperparameters deferred to supplementary; asset library construction not fully documented; 'brief dynamic simulation' duration undefined

Unquantified solver claims: 'High success rate for final validation' not quantified; assertion about pose sampling guarantees needs clarification regarding numerical precision; no computational cost or scalability analysis

Limited scope and generalization: Demonstrated only on indoor scenes; handling of articulated or deformable parts unexplored; DAG constraint may be restrictive (mutual support scenarios); generalization to other domains unclear

Small-scale user study: Only 20 participants evaluating 12 scenes each; no inter-rater reliability reported; missing quantitative generation metrics (collision rate, contact accuracy, physical stability)

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Part-level spatial relations address real ambiguities in preposition-based scene descriptions that object-level scene graphs cannot capture
Thoughtfully designed representation: The PAG formulation with two-level hierarchy (objects and parts), labeled oriented surfaces, and DAG constraint is elegant and computationally tractable

Substantial dataset contribution: PARSE-10K contains 10,000 scenes with 17,372 part-segmented objects across 132 categories and explicit part-level contact annotations, representing significant data collection effort
Multi-task validation: Framework demonstrates utility across VLM spatial reasoning and 3D scene generation, showing versatility
Strong quantitative results on target tasks: VLM achieves 97.4% on visual relation MCQ and scene generation shows user preference for complexity/fidelity
Clear presentation: Figures effectively communicate PAG structure and solver pipeline
weaknesses: Critical scalability bottleneck inadequately addressed: PAG construction is acknowledged as 'partially manual and sensitive to canonical poses' but the actual annotation pipeline from real images is not described. Without clarity on this process, reproducibility and practical impact are severely compromised. This fundamentally undermines claims of advancing spatial modeling beyond existing manual annotation approaches

Insufficient evidence for PAG representation advantages: Experiments do not isolate PAG's contribution. No ablations comparing PAG-conditioned generation against object-level scene graphs with equivalent supervision. VLM improvements could result from dataset quality, additional part-level supervision, or both—not necessarily PAG representation superiority

VLM evaluation concerns: 97.4% accuracy suggests overfitting to synthetic dataset. Generalization analysis vague ('added some manually labeled real images from COCO'—how many? performance split?). Baselines are general VLMs, not spatial-reasoning specialists. MCQ task with synthetic distractors may not reflect real challenges

Incomplete scene generation evaluation: User study limited (20 participants, 12 scenes); statistical significance unreported. Missing quantitative metrics: actual physical stability, contact accuracy, solver success rate, runtime. Only InstructScene baseline (trained on different data, confounding dataset/architecture differences). Unconditioned PARSE-10K variant produces 'unrealistic physics,' suggesting model-dataset mismatch
Limited contact model: Acknowledged limitation on oblique contacts; no systematic exploration of failure cases or analysis of contact accuracy in generated scenes

Insufficient dataset analysis: No quantitative distribution of spatial relation types, biases, or consistency. 49.9 avg. objects/scene appears artificially high. No formal evaluation of physical realism (what fraction stable after simulation?)

Reproducibility issues: Part library curation process unexplained (how 17,372 assets obtained/validated?). Solver hyperparameters (thresholds, tolerances, sampling strategies) incompletely specified. Runtime/computational cost not discussed. Code/data availability not mentioned

Generalization limitations: Only residential indoor scenes (17 room types); applicability to outdoor, commercial, or non-furniture objects unexplored. No analysis of category-specific failures or domain shift

Technical novelty of solver is moderate: Coarse localization is 2D region pruning; part-level alignment uses standard constraint-based geometry; final sampling is rejection sampling. Physics simulation via Sapien is off-the-shelf. Solver approach is incremental over existing constraint-based placement methods

strengths: Well-motivated representation: Clearly illustrates why part-level modeling is necessary through concrete examples (e.g., book cover vs. spine on table). The PAG design is thoughtful with labeled surfaces providing precise geometric interfaces.

Comprehensive system: Rather than isolated contributions, presents a complete pipeline from representation through constraint solver to physics validation and dataset generation. Strong integration of components.

Strong experimental results: VLM fine-tuning shows substantial improvements (97.4% vs. 82.1-86.2% on Visual Relation MCQ; 86.2% on Part-level Contact vs. 60.4-75.6% baselines). Scene generation user study shows 47.5% preference for PAG-conditioned vs. 7.5% baseline.

Valuable dataset contribution: PARSE-10K uniquely combines 10,000 scenes with dense part-level annotations and contact graphs. Significantly higher object density (49.9 avg vs. others) with systematic part segmentation across 132 categories.

Clear presentation: Well-written with effective visualizations. Figure 2 and 3 effectively communicate PAG structure and solving pipeline. Honest discussion of limitations demonstrates careful scholarship.
Principled DAG formulation: Ensures both physical realizability and computational tractability by enforcing unique support relations, enabling decomposition into localized subproblems.
Evaluation diversity: Tests across three distinct tasks (MCQ, contact MCQ, scene graph generation) and includes grounding-agnostic metrics that isolate relational reasoning from visual localization.
weaknesses: Insufficient clarity on PAG construction: The process of 'extracting layout priors from real images' is vague with no algorithmic details. Unclear if this is automated, semi-automatic, or manual; what annotation costs are involved; how to scale to new domains. This is critical for reproducibility.

Limited scene generation evaluation: Compared against only InstructScene baseline. No ablation studies on component importance (PAG-only vs. PAG+physics, object-level vs. part-level edges). User study is modest (20 participants × 12 scenes). Unclear why unconditioned variant performs poorly.

Real-image generalization not thoroughly evaluated: All main experiments use synthetic rendered scenes. Paper mentions adding 'some manually labeled real images from COCO' to test set but does not report separate real vs. synthetic performance metrics. For a paper on spatial reasoning, lack of real-world validation is concerning.

Scalability constraints of DAG structure: Requirement that each object has unique supporter is restrictive. Cannot represent physically realizable non-hierarchical contact patterns or cyclic dependencies. This design choice is acknowledged but not thoroughly justified.

Contact model limitations not quantified: Directional-face model fails on oblique surfaces, but no analysis of failure mode frequency or impact. Unclear what fraction of PARSE-10K contacts are oblique or how failures affect downstream tasks.

Limited technical novelty in solver: Core coarse-to-fine constraint satisfaction with physics refinement uses established techniques. Main contribution is applying these to part-level constraints, which is useful but algorithmically incremental. No comparison with alternative solving approaches.

Incomplete dataset analysis: Distribution of scenes across 17 room types not provided. Semantic object distribution unclear. Potential biases in synthetic generation not discussed. This limits understanding of representativeness.

Missing experimental details and ablations: Fine-tuning setup (learning rate, batch size, iterations) not specified. Scene generation architecture details sparse. No ablation studies on PAG component importance. Reproducibility is compromised.

strengths: Novel problem formulation addressing a genuine limitation in existing scene representations—the inability to capture fine-grained part-level interactions crucial for physical plausibility
Substantial PARSE-10K dataset contribution with 10,000 scenes, comprehensive part-level annotations, and explicit contact information, potentially enabling future research in spatial reasoning
Clear and well-designed Part-centric Assembly Graph (PAG) representation with intuitive hierarchical structure distinguishing object-level and part-level relations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple tasks (visual relation reasoning, contact understanding, scene graph generation) with strong baseline comparisons and user studies
Physical grounding through Sapien simulation ensures generated scenes satisfy physical constraints, providing practical utility
Well-organized presentation with detailed algorithms and extensive supplementary material supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty in the Part-Aware Spatial Configuration Solver—implements straightforward sequential constraint satisfaction without exploring more sophisticated optimization or solver techniques
Unclear part-level contact annotation acquisition process: no specification of manual vs. automatic annotation, consistency metrics, or inter-annotator agreement, raising scalability concerns
Scene generation results are incremental rather than compelling (SGG Recall 73.2%, Precision 76.6%, F1 78.2%), with limited reporting of generation success rates or failure analysis
Absence of systematic ablation studies on PAG components, solver stages, and sensitivity to annotation quality, limiting understanding of which elements drive improvements
Part taxonomy undefined for different object categories—no explicit definition of what constitutes a 'part,' consistency metrics, or category-level analysis despite 132 categories
User study compares only against InstructScene (a 2D-to-3D baseline); missing comparisons with recent scene generation methods, limiting understanding of competitive positioning
MCQ-based evaluation tasks (Visual Relation, Part-level Contact) are artificial; strong performance may not reflect broader spatial reasoning capabilities or generalization to open-ended scenarios
Insufficient analysis of failure cases, challenging scenarios, runtime/computational complexity, and which relation types or scene configurations pose difficulties
Limited scope of scene generation baseline comparisons—only InstructScene and 3D-FRONT included, missing other recent methods for full evaluation
Modest improvements on core tasks combined with limited technical novelty raise questions about practical significance beyond dataset contribution

strengths: Well-motivated problem: The paper clearly articulates why part-level spatial understanding is important and goes beyond object-level scene graphs for capturing fine-grained physical relationships.

Useful dataset contribution: PARSE-10K with 10,000 scenes and dense part-level annotations shows good diversity in object categories, room types, and spatial configurations—potentially valuable as a community resource.
Multi-task evaluation framework: Comprehensive evaluation across three complementary tasks (visual relation, part-level contact, scene graph generation) provides multiple validation angles.
Strong results on scene graph generation: Achieves 73.2/74.8 F1 score, substantially outperforming baseline models on the SGG task.
Reasonable hierarchical representation: The two-level PAG structure (object nodes, part nodes, coarse edges, fine edges) is a sensible design for part-aware spatial relationships.
weaknesses: Problematic baseline comparisons: VLM baselines (GPT-5, Gemini, Claude, Qwen3-VL) are fine-tuned on PARSE-10K itself, making them unfair comparisons. These general-purpose models were never designed for part-level reasoning. No comparison against these models without fine-tuning or against other part-aware methods.

Limited algorithmic novelty: The spatial configuration solver is essentially standard constraint satisfaction (topological sort, coarse-to-fine refinement, geometric reasoning). Scene generation applies existing diffusion models with standard techniques. Core novelty reduces to the PAG representation, which alone is insufficient for a top-tier venue.

Insufficient data quality validation: No quantitative quality metrics (inter-annotator agreement, ground-truth validation against real images). Contact extraction relies on many heuristics with unclear reproducibility. No comparison against real-world ground truth to validate annotation accuracy.

Severely limited user study: Only 3 scenes evaluated with human subjects—sample size too small for meaningful conclusions. Results are modest (45% contact fidelity even in controlled settings with PAG constraints).

Narrow scope and unclear generalization: Dataset limited to indoor furniture scenes with no analysis of generalization to other domains. Scene densities (avg. 49.9 objects) seem unrealistic. No cross-dataset validation against other scene understanding benchmarks.

Unablated design choices: No evidence that two-level PAG is superior to alternatives. Spatial relations set (Table 4) appears manually curated without clear justification. Edge representations using prepositions can be ambiguous when multiple relations apply.
Missing failure analysis: No discussion of when/why the method fails, what configurations violate assumptions, or how conflicting constraints are resolved.
Presentation density: Paper tries to cover representation + solver + dataset + multiple tasks simultaneously, diffusing focus and obscuring core technical contributions.
Weak scene generation validation: Figure 6 shows qualitative results without quantitative metrics. Whether generated scenes are correct and realistic beyond MCQ tasks is unclear.
Reproducibility concerns: Many implementation details missing or relegated to appendix. Manual verification steps introduce subjective bias. No commitment to releasing code/dataset.

strengths: Novel Part-Aware Relational Spatial Modeling (PAG) framework that effectively addresses limitations of existing scene graphs by explicitly capturing fine-grained part-level geometric relationships with well-motivated hierarchical design

Substantial high-quality dataset contribution (PARSE-10K): 10,000 densely annotated indoor scenes with full part-segmentation, averaging 49.9 objects/scene with explicit part-level contact annotations, providing valuable community resource
Strong quantitative results across multiple tasks: 97.4% on visual relation MCQ (vs 86% baseline), 86.2% on part-level contact (vs 60% baseline), 73.2% recall and 80.3% F1 on scene graph generation

Technically sophisticated and comprehensive solver pipeline with multi-stage constraint refinement (coarse localization → part-level alignment → fine-grained control → physics validation) demonstrated in clear algorithmic pseudocode

Excellent reproducibility support with detailed implementation specifications, hyperparameters, training procedures, dataset statistics, and clear visualizations effectively explaining PAG structure and solver methodology
Demonstrated framework versatility across visual reasoning, contact reasoning, and scene generation tasks showing generalizability within 3D scene understanding
weaknesses: Scene generation evaluation insufficient: only single baseline comparison (InstuctScene); missing comparisons with recent diffusion-based or learning-based generation methods; user study limited to 12 scenes; physics validation metrics not clearly reported; user ratings show modest 45% for physical realism

Missing critical ablation studies: no analysis isolating importance of part-level vs object-level edges; no systematic study of which relation types most critical; limited justification for solver architecture choices; no quantitative failure mode analysis

Scalability and computational efficiency unaddressed: no solver runtime timing analysis; performance degradation with scene complexity unclear; computational cost for feasibility solving not quantified; contradicts efficiency claims without evidence

Part-level relation taxonomy (22 types in Table 4) presented without analysis of frequency distribution, difficulty of enforcement, or ambiguous edge cases; unclear how algorithm handles over-constrained conflicting constraints

Dataset scope limitations: restricted to indoor scenes; uneven distribution across room types (meeting room only 8.3% of scenes); only 17 room types; reliance on expensive part-segmentation limits broader applicability

Limited experimental comparisons: spatial reasoning tasks only against general VLMs; recent graph-based and GPT-based scene generation methods in references not evaluated; no statistical significance testing on results

Physics validation concerns: sparse analysis in appendix; no breakdown of validation success rates by scene type or complexity; infeasibility rate and residual collision issues not quantified; Sapien simulator not validated against real-world physics

Technical clarity gaps: Algorithm 1 handling of conflicting constraints not specified; transition from relational control to geometric reasoning under-motivated; default vs explicit surface specifications confusingly explained; mechanism for constraint conflict resolution unclear
